"Stonking" is an informal British English adjective that means impressively large, powerful, or excellent. Think of it as a turbo-charged version of saying something is "really great" or "absolutely massive." It is used to add strong emphasis — to signal that something goes well beyond ordinary.

1. Meaning "enormous" or "very powerful/severe"

Here, "stonking" simply emphasizes that something is huge in size or intensity. The thing being described doesn't have to be good — it just has to be significant in degree.

  • "He had a stonking headache all morning."

(= a really bad, severe headache — not a mild one)

  • "She told a stonking lie to get out of trouble."

(= a really big, bold lie)

  • "There was a stonking great tree blocking the road."

(= an enormous tree)

2. Meaning "outstanding" or "excellent"

Here, "stonking" describes something that is impressively good — something that makes people take notice.

  • "That was a stonking performance on stage."

(= a truly outstanding, impressive performance)

  • "They got a stonking deal on the house."

(= a really great deal)

  • "She scored a stonking goal in the final minute."

(= a breathtaking, brilliant goal)
The single thing that connects both uses

Both meanings share one idea: "way beyond normal." Whether something is hugely bad, hugely impressive, or hugely good — "stonking" signals that it sits at the extreme end of its scale. It's never used for something ordinary or middling. You would never say "a stonking cup of tea" about an average cup of tea — only about one that was somehow spectacular.

"Stonking" is enthusiastic and lively. When someone uses it, they are not being dry or neutral — they are expressing energy and emphasis. It makes a sentence feel vivid and punchy. Native British speakers often use it the way someone might slam a hand on a table to make a point.

It is British slang, and it belongs firmly in informal, spoken, or casual written English (like in a newspaper sports column, a text message, or a friend's conversation). You would not use it in a formal essay, a business report, or an academic paper. It is rare in American English.

To help you feel the word rather than just understand it logically:

  • Imagine seeing a double rainbow filling the whole sky. Someone might say: "That's absolutely stonking!"
  • Imagine someone getting hit with an unexpected, enormous bill. They might say: "I got a stonking invoice in the post today."
  • A sports commentator watching a record-breaking athletic jump might shout: "That is a stonking leap!"

In each case, notice that the word amplifies — it tells you that the thing in question is far beyond what you'd ordinarily expect.

• It does not mean mediocre or just "quite good." It always signals something at a high intensity or impressive level.
  • It is not a rude or offensive word — it is perfectly acceptable in polite informal conversation.
  • It does not carry sarcasm on its own. If someone says "a stonking mistake," they genuinely mean it was a huge mistake — not that the mistake was secretly good.
One-sentence summary to anchor it in your memory
"Stonking" means impressively large, powerful, or excellent — it is an enthusiastic British intensifier used to say that something is far beyond the ordinary.
